The specific patent engine designed to bridge structured and unstructured data became the core product for Clarabridge. Because the software was designed to read open-ended text—like emails, transcripts, and online message boards—and structure it for analysis, it became incredibly appealing to the public sector.

The technology gave intelligence agencies the exact pipeline required to auto-analyze massive datasets for threat signals, sentiment tracking, and high-risk patterns.

While many specific contracts remain classified, Clarabridge actively marketed its text-mining and semantic-analysis tools to the federal intelligence community and homeland security agencies to screen massive volumes of text for risk detection and operational intelligence.

Federal entities and heavily regulated healthcare providers used these text analytics tools to audit compliance, process feedback, and parse unstructured electronic records.

When companies like Teradata acquired Claraview and Qualtrics eventually acquired Clarabridge, the public-sector data pipelines built on top of the original patent frameworks transitioned over into those enterprise platforms, where they continue to support municipal, state, and federal agencies today.

The technology is heavily linked to the CIA and the broader U.S. intelligence community. The specific operational implementations inside the Agency are classified, but the original patents were actively integrated into the national security apparatus.

Executive engineers act often act as specialized consultants to the CIA and other branches of the U.S. Intelligence Community. They advise agency leadership on how to deploy semantic text-mining tools, automate open-source intelligence (OSINT) gathering, and upgrade legacy database infrastructures to handle the influx of global digital communications.

Ultimately, because Clarabridge and Claraview were built in the Washington, D.C. contractor ecosystem, many early employees held the active security clearances required to work hand-in-hand with CIA analysts, translating raw software concepts into active counterterrorism and national security data pipelines.

The lineage of Clarabridge is heavily tied to MicroStrategy—the enterprise analytics giant where Clarabridge's co-founders worked early in their careers. MicroStrategy (now Strategy) has long been a core software staple used by aerospace and defense contractors to build operational and supply chain dashboards for the military.

Defense contractors frequently bundled Clarabridge's technology into the analytics packages they deployed for military commands.

Beyond intelligence gathering, defense contractors used these tools to fix messy military data pipelines. For example, when building out data management systems like the Enterprise Data Warehouse (EDW) models used by defense agencies, contractors used specialized ETL toolsets to synchronize massive inventories, maintenance logs, and field reports into a unified screen for commanders.

By operating as the specialized data engine inside the broader systems built by traditional military contractors, the technology effectively expanded its reach across the entire defense sector.

While Nithi Vivatrat’s original Clarabridge patent focused primarily on text analytics, Clarabridge eventually expanded its engine to include "Visual Listening" (image analysis) during Vivatrat’s tenure as Chief Product Officer. The company partnered with computer vision specialists to extract metadata from pictures (such as corporate logos or backgrounds) and pass them through an ETL layer so the information could be structured and analyzed alongside text data.

The primary bottleneck in modern UAP research—both for the government and civic science initiatives like Harvard's Galileo Project—is filtering out the massive noise of civilian air traffic, satellites, balloons, and weather phenomena. To find an "anomaly," an AI system must first structure raw visual data.

Military sensors (like those managed by the NRO) and high-resolution telescopes generate petabytes of raw video and multi-spectrum satellite imagery. 

Advanced Computer Vision (CV) networks and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) serve as the transformation layer. The AI scans thousands of hours of sky footage, automatically classifying known objects (e.g., matching the speed and thermal signature of a standard commercial drone or flight pattern).

The system isolates the statistical outliers—the truly "unidentified" targets that do not fit known aerodynamic or physical models—and loads them into a structured database for intelligence analysts or scientists to investigate.

By using neural networks to automate the "transformation" of raw imagery into clean structured metrics, defense systems and independent researchers can quickly weed out millions of false positives and focus exclusively on high-interest targets.

In March 2016, a new Clarabridge service has been developed through a partnership with image recognition specialist Ditto Labs, whose proprietary computer vision and machine learning technology automatically tags the brands, products, objects and environments which appear in the 1.8 billion photos shared across social media networks every day. 

Clarabridge clients could identify and analyze relevant photos, and engage with the people who post them in near real-time. It also made it possible for clients to extend their social media listening beyond keywords, to analyze photos and associated comments for insights using Clarabridge's text and sentiment analysis.

History: Before Clarabridge existed as a standalone software product, the technology’s founders and co-inventors (including Nithi Vivatrat) operated under Claraview, Inc., a business intelligence consulting firm founded in 2001. Claraview began securing data warehousing and text ETL contracts across federal and defense agencies—including parts of the Department of Defense (DoD)—throughout the post-9/11 technology boom of the early to mid-2000s.

Between 2006 and 2008, Clarabridge rapidly grew its text-analytics and visual-listening capabilities. During this timeframe, the company began marketing its technology to the federal market as a tool for screening Open Source Intelligence (OSINT) and parsing foreign text communications.

Rather than a direct, publicly announced contract from the CIA, early software implementations of this type typically bypass standard public bidding via two distinct paths:

• Early on, Clarabridge's text-mining software was frequently integrated into national security pipelines as a specialized tool bundled into massive software infrastructure packages by prime defense contractors like Lockheed Martin or Booz Allen Hamilton.

• The U.S. Intelligence Community frequently evaluates and acquires tech like Clarabridge via In-Q-Tel, the CIA's strategic venture capital arm. 

While Clarabridge itself was heavily backed by traditional commercial venture firms (like Grotech Ventures and Summit Partners), it routinely aligned its capabilities with intelligence community analytics criteria defined by these procurement pipelines.

Prime defense contractors routinely use specialized ETL engines as pre-processors for systems like Palantir. Raw, unorganized data cannot just be dumped directly into a graph-database environment like Palantir without breaking its performance. 

Contractors deploy automated text-mining pipelines to ingest raw data, clean it, extract the semantic meaning (names, places, context), and then load the clean, structured metadata directly into Palantir's visualization platforms for analysts to map out networks.

Palantir is essentially a "destination and visualization" platform, while a semantic ETL tool is the "factory" that prepares the raw material.

Defense contractors and federal agencies monitoring illicit finance sometimes use blockchain tracking tools to watch public Bitcoin ledger movements, while simultaneously using semantic text analytics (like Clarabridge's engine) to crawl dark-web forums, social media, and chat rooms. They then cross-reference the extracted text discussions with the physical wallet transactions. @leahfiles @ShawnRyan762 

Defense contractors rely on these specific ETL and analytics tools to solve two primary operational issues:

• Intelligence Ingestion (OSINT): Contractors build automated monitoring stations for military commands. These stations constantly pull in foreign news broadcasts, social media posts, and intercepted data. The ETL tool acts as an automated translator and filter, scanning the text to instantly isolate target keywords or sudden shifts in regional sentiment before routing the flagged data to human analysts.

• Military Logistics and Maintenance: Military vehicles, aircraft, and supply lines generate millions of pages of unstructured mechanics' notes, maintenance logs, and failure reports. Contractors pass these text logs through semantic analytics platforms to spot recurring mechanical failure trends across entire fleets before they cause active mission failures.

[Raw Unstructured Text] 
▼ [Step 1: The Pre-Cursor Tool (e.g., Clarabridge/ETL Engine)]   - Extracts raw data   - Translates text & analyzes sentiment   - Flags Entities (Names, Places, Dates)
 ▼ [Step 2: The Destination Platform (e.g., Palantir Gotham)]   - Links the entities together   - Visualizes network maps   - Enables analyst queries & tracking

Once inside Palantir, the software can instantly draw a visual line connecting Person A to Person B on a digital map. The analyst never has to read the millions of raw files; they just interact with the clean, connected intelligence map that the pre-cursor tool generated.

Palantir structures data using an Ontology. In data science, an ontology is a rigorous framework that defines how real-world objects, concepts, and relationships are categorized within a digital system.

By filtering that scraped data through a semantic ETL layer first, Palantir automatically translates chaotic internet chatter into the rigid Objects, Properties, and Links that Palantir needs to map out global threat networks.

One of the primary ways that UAP researchers have been targeted is via their relationships. @UAPSAC 

ETL modelers write the automated rules that tag data based on its source, classification level (e.g., Secret, Top Secret), and operational caveating.

If a raw intercept contains a U.S. citizen's private information, the ETL modeler builds a data transformation pipeline that automatically redacts or hashes that specific row of data before it reaches downstream users.

Traditional Defense Primes (Booz Allen Hamilton, CACI International, Leidos, SAIC) operate the physical data capture systems (satellites, cell towers, drone feeds) and deploy software to sanitize and drop unneeded data packets before feeding the high-value metadata into Palantir.

Hardware & Sensor Integrators like L3Harris Technologies and Sierra Nevada Corporation (SNC) handle the ruggedized sensor hardware. They filter out background noise, radio static, and telemetry clutter at the sensor level so Palantir receives clean targeting tracks.

In modern cloud environments, agencies build massive "data lakehouses" using Databricks or Snowflake to handle vast, raw ETL operations. Once billions of rows of logs are parsed, cleaned, and organized, the structured results are piped into Palantir's AI and Ontology layer to map out target behaviors.

Boutique tech agencies (like Claraview, historically) and system integrators embed directly with federal tech teams. They build custom data preparation scripts specifically designed to structure legacy government databases into a format that Palantir can digest without lagging.

By using this multi-layered approach, defense systems ensure that raw, chaotic global data is heavily refined, formatted, and strictly authorized.

Restricted Views (RVs): This is Palantir’s primary mechanism for row-level security. A Restricted View acts as a dynamic read-layer directly on top of a backing dataset. If a user belongs to a specific organizational group (e.g., "US Central Command"), the Restricted View automatically masks or deletes rows associated with other regions before the data ever reaches their screen.

Object and Property Security Policies: When data is transformed into an Ontology object (like a specific "Person" or "Vehicle"), administrators apply fine-grained policies. Property Security Policies act as column-level security—for instance, allowing all analysts to see a target's vehicle make and model, but restricting the license plate number column to individuals with elevated clearance.

Mandatory "Markings": These are cryptographic data tags that attach directly to data packets. Palantir’s core security advantage is provenance propagation—if a raw database row is tagged with a "Top Secret" marking, any downstream metric, chart, or combined dataset built from that row automatically inherits that exact same marking, blocking unauthorized users downstream.

The Tactical Intelligence Targeting Access Node (TITAN) is the U.S. Army's next-generation, AI-enabled mobile ground station designed to process massive battlefield sensor streams to dramatically reduce the "sensor-to-shooter" timeline.

Palantir Technologies: Oversees the overall program, manufacturing, and delivery. Natively embeds its software environment directly into the vehicle terminals to ingest space, aerial, and terrestrial radar and thermal feeds. Its software runs automated target recognition models to nominate targets directly to weapons systems.

Anduril Industries: Acts as a major partner, receiving a large portion of the hardware budget to construct the ruggedized physical shelters and execute the hardware-to-vehicle integration for the mobile ground units.

L3Harris Technologies & Sierra Nevada Corporation (SNC): Responsible for integrating sensor capabilities. They build the interface data pipelines that capture real-time feeds from electronic surveillance aircraft, drones, and military satellites, normalizing the raw imagery signals before sending them to Palantir's processor.

For counter-drone (C-UAS) systems like the VAMPIRE platform, L3Harris embeds computer vision tech licensed from Shield AI. This specialized neural network uses passive EO/IR video feeds to detect, classify, and track distant, small unmanned aerial systems, even when they are heavily obscured by clouds, trees, or buildings.

https://t.co/XoziqrIdm6 Vision Engine: For maritime and naval autonomous vessels, L3Harris integrates its ASView system with https://t.co/XoziqrIdm6’s predictive computer vision models to execute autonomous vessel tracking and maritime "pattern-of-life" detection.

Strategic Technology Consulting (STC) & World Wide Technology (WWT): Provide the underlying tactical communication networks, cyber security baselines, and commercial network infrastructure required to keep the mobile ground stations connected to the wider military grid in active combat zones.

SNC’s primary computer vision focus is cross-domain sensor fusion—blending traditional visual imagery with radar and laser tracking so computer systems or pilots can navigate in zero-visibility conditions. Their primary tech stack includes:

• Sierra Fusion (3D World Model)
• Degraded Visual Environment Pilotage System (DVEPS)
• Seekr AI Foundational Models
• SNC TRAX Software Suite: A JADC2-enabled multi-domain platform deployed across dozens of military sensors and weapons systems that translates computer vision classifications into actionable target telemetry.

To make computer vision work in austere combat zones where cloud connectivity is non-existent, L3Harris takes a decentralized approach. Instead of building massive, bloated AI frameworks, they rely on embedded edge processing optimized for ultra-low latency.

Edge Hardware Acceleration: These models are deployed inside WESCAM pods using ruggedized, low-power graphics processing chips, such as NVIDIA Jetson modules or customized Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs). Because the processing happens right next to the camera lens, the system can automatically lock onto and track multiple moving combatants or vehicles simultaneously, without needing to transmit any video data back to a central server.

How SNC’s Sierra Fusion Constructs 3D Flight Maps

Sierra Nevada Corporation's Sierra Fusion architecture addresses a critical tactical problem: how do you pilot a helicopter or land a transport plane when a sandstorm, thick smoke, or heavy fog completely blinds the pilot?

Rather than relying on a single camera, Sierra Fusion acts as a real-time sensor-fusion computer vision engine that builds a live, digital 3D model of the terrain. @AshtonForbes

find a competitor's most controversial feature.

controversy gets attention, but solving the complaint gives people a reason to follow you.

do the same thing with your content.

announce each new format, measure the response, and keep the ones that attract buyers.

find 20 small creators whose audiences already match the product.

offer them a custom AI video or playable challenge they can post, with a revenue share on any sales they generate.

they get new content without paying upfront. you get access to an audience you haven't built yet.

repeat with different niches until you find one that converts.

Opera wants websites to run AI on your laptop instead of sending your data to the cloud | Paulo Vargas, Digital Trends

Opera wants to move routine AI work out of distant data centers and onto the computer already sitting on your desk. Its new WebAI preview lets websites and browser extensions use local models inside Opera One without requiring another AI subscription or sending the information they handle to a cloud service.

WebAI also opens local AI to third-party developers instead of reserving it for Opera’s own features. Your laptop supplies the computing power, provided it has enough to spare.

How WebAI puts models to work

WebAI is a proposed web standard that gives websites and extensions access to AI through the browser. Opera says the effort has backing from Google and Microsoft. Its implementation is model-agnostic and centered on open models.

Opera One can tap Google’s Gemma models, while compatible Macs can also use Apple’s on-device foundation model. Developers can generate or classify text without maintaining their own AI servers or paying for every request sent to an outside service.

Opera’s examples are deliberately practical and a little nosy. One extension can sort a messy tab collection, while another can flag clickbait before it eats another five minutes of your life.

What stays under your control

Opera has kept WebAI disabled by default. Nothing is downloaded until the user enables it, and each site needs permission before it can access the browser’s local AI. That extra layer is important when websites, rather than only Opera, can call the models running on your computer.

No data center will rescue weaker hardware, however. Speed and capability depend on the computer, and Opera hasn’t disclosed minimum performance requirements beyond the supported platforms. Opera GX and Opera Neon are scheduled to receive WebAI later.

Why Opera also built a bulldozer

Opera is pairing WebAI with a separate experiment called HTML-in-Canvas. It lets developers place functional webpages inside 2D and 3D scenes, where buttons and forms keep working as the page moves through virtual space.

The showcase includes a Gamer Room with live webpages on its screens and Webpage Bulldozer, which turns site elements into objects you can shove around. Both demos already work in Opera browsers without setup, so the bulldozer is the part anyone can try while WebAI remains an opt-in early preview.

Should a diffusion model in online RL be the policy, or the thing that proposes plans?

GTP (Generative Trajectory Planning; Harvard, NeurIPS 2026) argues for the second. Like TD-MPC2, it plans through learned dynamics, reward and value models, but the candidate action sequences come from a diffusion prior instead of Gaussian sampling.

Beam search refines the candidates by partially re-noising and denoising them, and the best plans are distilled back into the prior, so search and proposals improve each other. When acting, the agent plans optimistically across a dynamics ensemble; when building value targets, it plans conservatively.

• Locomotion: highest mean return on all five Gym MuJoCo tasks after 1M steps, e.g. Humanoid 6,660 vs 5,269 for the best baseline; on Ant it is level with TD-MPC2

• Manipulation: on PushT from pixels it reaches 99% after 1M steps, while TD-MPC2 needs 3M steps to reach 97% and SAC and DreamerV3 stay at 0%

• Cost: action selection is on par with TD-MPC2 (34 vs 36 ms on an RTX 5090), but a training update takes 157 ms vs 4 ms, or 19 ms when planned trajectories are reused

• Deployment: the trained prior alone, without any search, keeps 99% success on FetchPickAndPlace at 8.6 ms per action
